blocks.body:
In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown watched tiny particles released from pollen grains jiggle ceaselessly in water. In 1905 Einstein explained the motion as the result of countless collisions with water molecules and predicted that the mean squared displacement grows linearly in time; measurements of this growth by Perrin helped convince physicists that atoms are real. Mathematically, the jiggling particle is the limit of a random walk whose steps become very small and very frequent, and the limit object, Brownian motion, is the most important random process in mathematics.

This page builds Brownian motion from the random walk, shows how wild its paths are, proves the reflection principle and explains the link with the heat equation. It uses the central limit theorem from [[limit-theorems]] and discrete [[martingales]].

blocks.title: Rescaling a random walk
blocks.body:
Let $S_k$ be simple random walk, with independent steps $\pm1$, each with probability $\tfrac12$. After $k$ steps it has mean $0$ and variance $k$, so its typical distance from the start is $\sqrt k$: about $10$ after $100$ steps, about $100$ after $10{,}000$. To see a limit we must shrink space by $\sqrt n$ when we speed up time by $n$. Define
$$W^{(n)}(t) = \frac{S_{\lfloor nt\rfloor}}{\sqrt n}, \qquad t \ge 0.$$
For fixed $t$, the central limit theorem says that $W^{(n)}(t)$ converges in distribution to $N(0, t)$. For $s < t$, the increment $W^{(n)}(t) - W^{(n)}(s)$ is built from steps disjoint from those making up $W^{(n)}(s)$, so in the limit increments over disjoint time intervals are independent normals with variance equal to the length of the interval. Any other scaling, such as dividing by $n$ or by $n^{1/3}$, gives a limit that is identically $0$ or does not exist. The square root is forced.

blocks.title: Brownian motion
Existence and the invariance principle
blocks.body:
1. (Wiener, 1923.) Brownian motion exists. One construction: with $Z_0, Z_1, Z_2, \dots$ independent $N(0,1)$,
$$B_t = Z_0\,t + \sqrt2\sum_{k=1}^\infty Z_k\,\frac{\sin(k\pi t)}{k\pi}, \qquad 0 \le t \le 1,$$
converges uniformly on $[0,1]$ with probability $1$ and defines a Brownian motion on $[0,1]$; independent copies can be glued end to end to cover all $t \ge 0$.
2. (Donsker's invariance principle.) If the steps of the walk are any independent, identically distributed variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, the linearly interpolated paths $W^{(n)}$ converge in distribution to $B$ as random continuous functions. In particular, $E[\Phi(W^{(n)})] \to E[\Phi(B)]$ for every bounded continuous functional $\Phi$ of paths on $[0,1]$, for example $\Phi(w) = g\big(\max_{t \le 1} w(t)\big)$ with $g$ bounded and continuous. Both parts are stated without proof.

blocks.title: Why the construction works, and why it matters
blocks.body:
The series in part 1 is a [[fourier-series|Fourier sine series]] with random coefficients. It is a Gaussian process, so it is determined by its covariance, and the covariance is right because
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{2\sin(k\pi s)\sin(k\pi t)}{k^2\pi^2} = \min(s, t) - st \quad (0 \le s, t \le 1),$$
the sine expansion of the "tent" function; adding $Z_0 t$ contributes $st$, giving $\operatorname{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = \min(s,t)$. The proof is completed by checking uniform convergence, which takes real work, and we omit it.

Donsker's theorem is why Brownian motion is universal: whatever the step distribution, a long walk looks Brownian from far away, just as the central limit theorem makes sums look normal. Questions about long walks (the largest excursion, the time spent positive) can therefore be answered by computing once for $B$.

blocks.title: Basic properties
blocks.body:
From the definition, directly:

- Covariance: for $s \le t$, $E[B_sB_t] = E[B_s^2] + E[B_s(B_t - B_s)] = s$. So $\operatorname{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = \min(s, t)$.
- Scaling: for $c > 0$, $c^{-1/2}B_{ct}$ is again a standard Brownian motion. Zooming in by a factor $c$ in time and $\sqrt c$ in space gives the same picture, so the paths are statistically self-similar.
- Symmetry and time inversion: $-B_t$ is a Brownian motion, and so is $tB_{1/t}$ (set to $0$ at $t = 0$).
- Markov property: for fixed $s$, $(B_{s+t} - B_s)_{t \ge 0}$ is a Brownian motion independent of $(B_u)_{u \le s}$. The strong Markov property (stated here without proof) says the same holds when $s$ is replaced by a stopping time such as the first time $B$ hits a level.
- Martingales: with $\mathcal F_s$ the information in $(B_u)_{u \le s}$, the processes $B_t$, $B_t^2 - t$ and $e^{\theta B_t - \theta^2 t/2}$ are martingales, by the same calculation as for $S_n$, $S_n^2 - n$ and the exponential martingale of the random walk.

blocks.title: Quadratic variation
blocks.body:
For $t > 0$ and partitions $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = t$ with mesh $\max_k(t_k - t_{k-1}) \to 0$,
$$Q_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \left(B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}\right)^2 \longrightarrow t \quad \text{in mean square}.$$
Consequently, with probability $1$ the path has infinite total variation on every interval. In fact (Paley, Wiener and Zygmund) with probability $1$ the path is differentiable at no point.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $\Delta_k = t_k - t_{k-1}$. The increments are independent with $(B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}})^2 = \Delta_k Z_k^2$, where $Z_k \sim N(0,1)$. Since $E[Z^2] = 1$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z^2) = 2$,
$$E[Q_n] = \sum \Delta_k = t, \qquad E\left[(Q_n - t)^2\right] = \operatorname{Var}(Q_n) = 2\sum_k \Delta_k^2 \le 2t\max_k\Delta_k \to 0.$$
For the consequence, $Q_n \le \max_k|B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}|\cdot\sum_k|B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}|$. Pass to a subsequence of partitions along which $Q_n \to t > 0$ almost surely. The maximum tends to $0$ by uniform continuity of the path on $[0,t]$, so the sum, which is at most the total variation, must tend to infinity. The same argument on each of the countably many intervals with rational endpoints (the increments of $B$ over $[r, r']$ form a Brownian motion run for time $r' - r$) gives infinite variation on all of them at once with probability $1$, hence on every interval. The nowhere-differentiability theorem needs a finer argument, which we omit.

blocks.title: Rough paths and a new calculus
blocks.body:
For a smooth function, the sum of squared increments over a fine partition tends to $0$; for Brownian motion it tends to $t$. Heuristically $(dB)^2 = dt$: over a time $\Delta$ the path moves about $\sqrt\Delta$, which is much larger than $\Delta$, so the slope $\Delta B/\Delta$ is of size $\Delta^{-1/2}$ and blows up. This is why calculus with Brownian motion needs new rules. In Itô's calculus, the extra term from $(dB)^2 = dt$ gives
$$\int_0^t B_s\,dB_s = \tfrac12\left(B_t^2 - t\right),$$
not the $\tfrac12 B_t^2$ that ordinary calculus would suggest; notice that the right side is the martingale $\tfrac12(B_t^2 - t)$.

blocks.title: Reflection principle
blocks.body:
For $a > 0$ and $t > 0$,
$$P\left(\max_{0 \le s \le t} B_s \ge a\right) = 2P(B_t \ge a) = 2\left(1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt t}\right)\right),$$
where $\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function. Equivalently, $\max_{s \le t}B_s$ has the same distribution as $|B_t|$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $T_a$ be the first time $B$ reaches $a$; then $\max_{s \le t}B_s \ge a$ exactly when $T_a \le t$. On this event, by the strong Markov property, the path after $T_a$ is a Brownian motion started at $a$, independent of the past, and so is its mirror image in the level $a$. Reflecting the part after $T_a$ therefore maps Brownian paths with $T_a \le t$ to Brownian paths with $T_a \le t$ and preserves probability; it exchanges paths ending above $a$ with paths ending below $a$. Hence
$$P(T_a \le t,\ B_t < a) = P(T_a \le t,\ B_t > a) = P(B_t > a),$$
the last step because $B_t > a$ forces $T_a \le t$ by continuity. Adding $P(T_a \le t, B_t \ge a) = P(B_t \ge a)$ and using $P(B_t = a) = 0$ gives the result.

For simple random walk the same argument is an exact bijection of paths: for integers $a \ge 1$, $P(\max_{k \le n}S_k \ge a) = P(S_n \ge a) + P(S_n > a)$.

blocks.title: Brownian motion and the heat equation
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be bounded and continuous and set $u(t, x) = E[f(x + B_t)]$, the expected value of $f$ at the position of a Brownian particle started at $x$. Since $x + B_t \sim N(x, t)$,
$$u(t, x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(y)\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}e^{-(y - x)^2/(2t)}\,dy,$$
and differentiating the kernel shows that
$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac12\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}, \qquad u(0, x) = f(x).$$
The transition density of Brownian motion is the heat kernel: the density of a cloud of Brownian particles spreads exactly as heat does, which is the content of Einstein's analysis. In several dimensions the same holds with the Laplacian, and the probability that Brownian motion started at $x$ leaves a region through a given part of the boundary is a harmonic function of $x$; this solves the Dirichlet problem for the [[laplace-equation]].
Find the distribution of $B_1 + B_2$, and compute $P(B_1 > 0,\ B_2 > 0)$.
blocks.solution:
$B_1 + B_2 = 2B_1 + (B_2 - B_1)$ is a sum of independent normals, with variance $4\cdot1 + 1 = 5$, so $B_1 + B_2 \sim N(0, 5)$.

For the probability, condition on $B_1 = x > 0$: then $B_2 = x + (B_2 - B_1)$ with an independent $N(0,1)$ increment, so $P(B_2 > 0 \mid B_1 = x) = \Phi(x)$. Hence
$$P(B_1 > 0, B_2 > 0) = \int_0^\infty \Phi(x)\varphi(x)\,dx = \left[\tfrac12\Phi(x)^2\right]_0^\infty = \tfrac12\left(1 - \tfrac14\right) = \tfrac38.$$
Positive correlation between $B_1$ and $B_2$ makes this larger than the $\tfrac14$ we would get for independent variables.

blocks.body: Find the probability that a standard Brownian motion exceeds $1$ at some time before $t = 1$, and show that the first hitting time $T_a$ of a level $a > 0$ is finite with probability $1$ but has infinite mean.
blocks.solution:
By the reflection principle, $P(\max_{s \le 1}B_s \ge 1) = 2(1 - \Phi(1)) \approx 0.3173$.

More generally $P(T_a \le t) = 2(1 - \Phi(a/\sqrt t))$, which tends to $2(1 - \Phi(0)) = 1$ as $t \to \infty$, so $T_a < \infty$ almost surely. For large $t$,
$$P(T_a > t) = 2\Phi\!\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt t}\right) - 1 = 2\int_0^{a/\sqrt t}\varphi(z)\,dz \ge \frac{2a}{\sqrt t}\,\varphi(a) \quad (t \ge 1),$$
using $\varphi(z) \ge \varphi(a)$ on $[0, a/\sqrt t] \subseteq [0, a]$. Since $\int_1^\infty t^{-1/2}\,dt = \infty$, $E[T_a] = \int_0^\infty P(T_a > t)\,dt = \infty$. The Brownian particle will certainly reach $a$, but on average it takes forever, exactly like the simple random walk waiting to reach $1$.

blocks.body: Let $a, b > 0$ and let $\tau$ be the first time $B$ leaves the interval $(-a, b)$. Find $P(B_\tau = b)$ and $E[\tau]$.
blocks.solution:
This is gambler's ruin in continuous time, and the optional stopping theorem holds for Brownian martingales under the same kind of conditions as in discrete time (a fact we use without proof). $B_{t \wedge \tau}$ is bounded by $\max(a, b)$, and $\tau < \infty$ almost surely (it is at most $T_b$), so $E[B_\tau] = 0$. If $p = P(B_\tau = b)$, then $pb - (1 - p)a = 0$ and
$$P(B_\tau = b) = \frac{a}{a + b}.$$
Next, $B_t^2 - t$ is a martingale, so $E[B_{t \wedge \tau}^2] = E[t \wedge \tau]$. Letting $t \to \infty$ (bounded convergence on the left, monotone convergence on the right),
$$E[\tau] = E[B_\tau^2] = \frac{a}{a+b}\,b^2 + \frac{b}{a+b}\,a^2 = ab.$$
Compare the random walk answer $a(N - a)$ for the walk started at $a$ in $[0, N]$: it is the same formula after shifting the start to $0$.

blocks.body:
- Displacement grows like $\sqrt t$, not like $t$. Doubling the time multiplies the typical distance by $\sqrt2$.
- $dB_t/dt$ does not exist, so equations "with white noise" need Itô's calculus; the ordinary chain rule fails, as $\int_0^t B\,dB = \tfrac12(B_t^2 - t)$ shows.
- Properties 1 to 3 of the definition do not by themselves give continuous paths; continuity is a separate requirement, and existence of a process with all four properties is a theorem.
- Optional stopping needs conditions here too: $E[B_{T_1}] = 1 \ne 0$ although $B$ is a martingale, because $T_1$ has infinite mean and $B$ is unbounded below before $T_1$.
- In the discrete reflection principle the boundary term matters: $P(\max S_k \ge a) = P(S_n \ge a) + P(S_n > a)$, not $2P(S_n \ge a)$.

Brownian motion is the continuous-time [[martingales|martingale]] par excellence and the scaling limit of the random walks of [[markov-chains]] and [[limit-theorems]]. Its transition density is the kernel of the [[heat-equation]], and exit distributions solve the Dirichlet problem for the [[laplace-equation]]; in two dimensions, Brownian paths are invariant under [[conformal-maps]] up to a time change, which gives probabilistic proofs of results in complex analysis. Simulating Brownian paths by [[monte-carlo]] is the standard way to evaluate expectations in stochastic models, including option prices in the Black–Scholes model, where a stock price is $S_0e^{\sigma B_t + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}$. The Fourier-series construction connects it with [[fourier-series]] and [[hilbert-spaces]] (an orthonormal expansion with independent Gaussian coefficients).

1. Show that $X_t = tB_{1/t}$ (with $X_0 = 0$) has the covariance $\min(s,t)$ of Brownian motion.
2. Show that $P(B_s > 0 \text{ for all } s \in (0, \varepsilon]) = 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$. (Hint: use scaling and the reflection principle on $-B$.)
3. Use the exponential martingale with $\theta = \sqrt{2\lambda}$ and optional stopping to show $E[e^{-\lambda T_a}] = e^{-a\sqrt{2\lambda}}$ for $\lambda > 0$.
4. For simple random walk, verify the discrete reflection identity $P(\max_{k \le 4}S_k \ge 2) = P(S_4 \ge 2) + P(S_4 > 2)$ by listing paths.
